Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
35-year-old male lawyer with new-onset frontal headaches, palpitations, arm tingling, mild weight loss, and decreased libido since starting a new job; advised in-person review and thyroid panel.

History:
• Presenting complaints: Intermittent frontal headaches (mainly at work), occasional palpitations (≈1×/day), bilateral arm tingling, episodic shortness of breath, reduced appetite, ~5 lb unintentional weight loss, diminished libido.  
• Onset/Duration: All symptoms began after recent job change; exact timeframe not stated.  
• Aggravating factors: Occur predominantly while working at computer or in meetings.  
• Associated symptoms: Mild nausea with headaches; denies leg tingling; no exertional dyspnea.  
• Stress level: Rates work stress 7–8/10.  
• Past medical history: Hyperthyroidism.  
• Medications: Thyroxine – dose/route/frequency not documented (see conflict).  
• Allergies: Not documented.  
• Social: Alcohol ~2 glasses wine weekly; non-smoker; denies recreational drug use.  
• Preventive care: Not discussed.

Examination:
• (No physical examination performed during tele-visit.)

Impression:
Multiple new symptoms (headache, palpitations, paresthesias, mild weight loss, decreased libido) temporally related to job change. Differential includes thyroid dysfunction, stress/anxiety-related disorders, and other metabolic or neurologic causes.

Plan:
• Arrange in-person clinic appointment for full physical examination (heart, respiratory, neurologic).  
• Order blood tests, including thyroid function tests.  
• No new medications until in-person assessment.  
• Patient to book appointment via clinic app; clinician will forward today’s history to next provider.  
• No further questions from patient.

Quality checks:

● Missing/expected elements:
  – Vitals not obtained.  
  – Allergies not documented.  
  – Medication dose/route/frequency for thyroxine not documented.  
  – Full review of systems, neurological history, family history not elicited.

● Internal conflicts:
  – Patient states diagnosis of “hyperthyroidism” yet reports taking “thyroxine” (typically used for hypothyroidism) – conflict noted.

● Transcript quality: Clear overall; occasional pauses/interruptions but clinically understandable.
